file: China_s Plans to Make Family Car Are Receding, Official Says.txt
text:
ï»¿
China's "family car" project, an idea that got Western auto makers salivating when they were invited to submit prototypes last year, is likely to be delayed until well into the next century, a senior Chinese official said today.
In the first public comments on the family car by a senior member of China's car bureaucracy since last fall, Huang Fuheng, general manager of the China National Automotive Industry Sales Corporation, said that making family cars salable would be a "very long and very complicated" process.
"It's going to be 10 or 15 years before a family car becomes feasible in China," Mr. Huang said in an interview. 
"It's a complicated process, not something that we can do in a day."
When Beijing held an exhibition for 20 leading foreign car makers last September, some officials suggested China would choose a single model, and could start producing them within five years.
Ford Motor Company recommended a model from its Fiesta line in Europe. 
Mitsubishi of Japan offered a mini-van while General Motors pushed a Corsa model from Adam Opel, its German subsidiary.
But Chinese auto officials fell silent after the exhibition, causing confusion among car makers. 
Mr. Huang's comments, coming shortly after an internal Government meeting on the family car project, indicated that car officials are divided about how to proceed.
"There are some people in our planning departments who favor a single model," Mr. Huang said. 
"My idea is that the family car should not be done in one factory, or in one model. 
There are several different kinds of cars needed in China."
He also conceded that it would be hard to meet the original demands set out by Chinese car bureaucrats: that it will be modern, with air-conditioning and anti-lock brakes, be fuel-efficient and cost less than $10,000.
"If you make a car that's too old a model, no one will want it; if you make it fully modern, it will be too expensive," he said.
The vast majority of the 1.4 million vehicles made in China last year were trucks; passenger cars totaled only 250,000, and most of those were purchased by Government work units, which can afford a $30,000-$50,000 sedan for their senior officials.
Chinese officials said last year that they want to consolidate the domestic market -- now composed of 120 or so small, inefficient plants making trucks -- into a handful of large companies that can push total production to 3 million by 2000, with more than a million of them cars. 
By 2010, they said, China should be producing 8 million vehicles, making it the world's second-largest auto market, after the United States.
Their comments, and China's booming economy persuaded several foreign auto makers that it was time to enter the Chinese market seriously. 
Yet the market they are entering is plagued by a poor supply network, an inexperienced labor force, and high tariffs that limit imports of autos and parts.
Foreign auto executives said today that Mr. Huang's comments clarified a situation they had already begun to sense: that priority is likely to be given to building a car component industry, and that plans for several new passenger car projects will be pared down.
"The family car is definitely way down the line," said Stephanie Hallford, a Ford executive in China. 
"For him to say that is not really out of context from what we've understood."

file: COMPANY NEWS_AID TO CHINA_S AUTO INDUSTRY IS PLANNED.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Japanese auto maker Toyota plans to help China's fledgling auto industry by sharing managerial expertise and technology, the company's president, Tatsuro Toyoda, said yesterday in Beijing. 
After meeting with the Chinese Prime Minister, Li Peng, Mr. Toyoda also said his company hoped to begin making cars in China in 1996. 
Mr. Toyoda did not provide details of a planned assembly plant, saying the project would be decided by the Chinese Government and Chinese partners. 
But Japanese news media reported that Toyota planned to begin a large-scale manufacturing project with Tianjin Automotive Industrial Group. 
Tianjin Automotive currently assembles cars under an agreement with the Daihatsu Motor Corporation, a small-car maker affiliated with Toyota.

file: COMPANY NEWS_HONDA TO START NEW VENTURE IN CHINA.txt
text:
ï»¿
Just three weeks after the Chinese Government began cracking down on runaway economic growth, the Honda Motor Company is shrugging off concerns of an economic squeeze to move ahead with its first passenger car production agreement in China. 
The Japanese auto maker said yesterday that it had signed an accord with the Yancheng Automobile Company of Guangzhou, near Hong Kong, to assemble Civic sedan passenger cars at Yancheng's existing factory, beginning in November.

file: COMPANY NEWS_JOINT VENTURE IN CHINA TO MANUFACTURE PUMPS.txt
text:
ï»¿
The ITT Corporation said yesterday that it had agreed to form a joint venture in China to manufacture sewage pumps and mining pumps. 
ITT will have a 65 percent stake in the venture with the Jinbei Automobile Company of Shenyang, China. 
The new company will employ about 100 people and make about 15,000 pumps a year, according to Leif E. Carlsson, the president of ITT Flygt A.B., a Swedish unit of ITT. 
Jinbei, which employs 40,000 people, is the 35th-largest industrial enterprise in China.

ï»¿
Daimler-Benz A.G. said today that it had started a joint venture with a Chinese partner to manufacture buses. 
The new company, to be based in Guangzhou province, will be called Yaxing-Benz and will be the largest Asian bus manufacturer. 
Daimler-Benz and Guangzhou Motor Coach Manufacturer each hold 50 percent in the joint venture. 
Yaxing-Benz will build 8,500 buses a year.

ï»¿
Deere & Company, the world's largest maker of tractors and combines, said this week that it had formed a joint venture with the Tianjin Tractor Manufacturing Company to improve sales by expanding geographically. 
Deere will own 51 percent of the John Deere Tiantuo Company, which will make and sell four models of tractors in China. 
The companies jointly invested about $21 million in the venture, which is based 100 miles southeast of Beijing in Tianjin, China.

file: G.M. Advances in Bid for China Venture.txt
text:
ï»¿
The General Motors Corporation has been named the top candidate in competition to negotiate a joint venture with the Chinese Government to build small cars in China, the company said today.
General Motors and the Beijing Government recently signed a memorandum of understanding that essentially makes the company the sole negotiating partner for the venture, a G.M. spokesman, Michael Meyerand, said.
Honda Motor, Hyundai of South Korea and the German auto makers BMW and the Mercedes-Benz unit of Daimler-Benz were competing for the project. 
It would provide a major foothold in what is expected to become one of the world's fastest-growing and largest automotive markets in the next century.
If successful, G.M.'s Opel AG European subsidiary will probably operate its end of the 50-50 joint venture. 
It is expected to build Opel Corsas or Astras, although the exact product is subject to negotiation, the G.M. spokesman said.
The product could end up being a variant of the new mini-car that G.M. this week said it planned to build in Brazil for the South American market, he said.
Production could reach as many as 100,000 units a year. 
The project would involve updating a plant in the southern city of Guangzhou. 
Peugeot Citroen, which holds a 22 percent stake in the plant, has been seeking to leave the venture.
G.M.'s project, if approved, would be the auto maker's third major production operation in China. 
It has a truck-assembly joint venture that is under construction in the northeastern city of Shenyang, and it recently got approval for a $1 billion joint venture scheduled to begin building midsize Buick sedans in Shanghai in late 1998.

ï»¿
GE Plastics is building a $50 million plant in China to sell its goods to that growing market. 
The Pittsfield-based division of the General Electric Company makes high-performance thermoplastics for cars, computers, telephones and other goods. 
The plant in the southern Chinese city of Nansha will be able to produce 20,000 tons of thermoplastics a year. 
It will be GE Plastics' first plant in China.

ï»¿
Chinese authorities have approved the Goodyear Tire and Rubber Company's venture with Dalian Rubber General Factory, the company said today. 
Goodyear said it would invest about $30 million to upgrade Dalian's machinery and processes and increase production of radial auto tires from a million tires a year to 1.4 million.

ï»¿
The Honda Motor Company, Japan's third-largest auto maker, said today that it would open about 100 sales outlets in China by April 2001 as it starts producing cars in China, the world's most populous country. 
Honda will open 30 outlets jointly with Chinese automobile dealers next month when Chinese production of the midsize Accord sedan begins, Yuzuru Matsuno, a Honda spokesman, said. 
Production will be at Honda's factory in Guangzhou, where the company expects to produce 100,000 Accords by 2001.

file: Honda, Beating Out G.M., Plans to Build Cars in China.txt
text:
ï»¿
Beating out a competing bid by the General Motors Corporation, the Honda Motor Company announced today that it had won the right to manufacture passenger cars at a plant in southern China.
Honda executives said the venture, their first auto assembly operation in China's perplexing car market, would involve a $200 million investment with two local partners to produce a model resembling the Honda Accord. 
Honda will take a 50 percent stake.
Yet Honda is essentially betting it can succeed where the French auto maker PSA Peugeot Citroen failed. 
Honda plans to use the same plant in Guangzhou that Peugeot vacated early this year, frustrated by low output, rising debt and squabbles with its local partner.
Honda executives, like their counterparts at other auto makers, expressed faith that the long-term potential in China's passenger car market was worth the considerable near-term difficulties, like bureaucratic interference, inadequate sourcing and an insular distribution network.
"We believe the Chinese market has the potential for further expansion in the future," Yoshihide Munekuni, Honda's chairman, told a news conference in Tokyo. 
"We will study the possibility of exports from the Chinese plant in the future."
General Motors expressed disappointment, but said it would not affect a larger commitment to G.M.'s $1.5 billion plant now under construction in Shanghai, where it plans to produce Buicks in 18 months.
"We regret that it was not possible for Opel/G.M. to reach agreement with the authorities in Guangzhou," G.M. said. 
"We believe our proposal, which provided a substantial investment in Guangzhou, would have been a viable business opportunity for all parties concerned."
Honda's local partners are the Guangzhou Auto Group Corporation, which Peugeot executives blamed for making their venture more trouble than it was worth, and the Dongfeng Motor Corporation, already a partner with Honda at a plant that produces engine and suspension components for export to other Honda plants in Asia.
The new Honda venture plans to start modestly, calling for just 30,000 vehicles a year. 
The first cars will be assembled in late 1999, Honda said.
The new venture will also give Honda its first automobile sales channel in the Chinese market, Mr. Munekuni said in Tokyo, where the No. 3 Japanese auto maker's plans were announced together with an upbeat earnings report timed to coincide with a visit to Japan by China's Prime Minister, Li Peng. 
Honda said earnings rose 33 percent in the six months ended Sept. 
30, powered by strong exports to the United States and Europe.
Mr. Munekuni promised that the new venture would not assume Guangzhou Auto's existing debt, though its size was not disclosed.
"Debts of Guangzhou Peugeot Automobile will be settled by the Guangzhou government," he said.
The first step in a long series of approvals that Honda must win, the Honda chairman added, is to apply to the central Government for permission to start a feasibility study on the venture. 
Formal approval of the venture will follow at a later date, barring insurmountable obstacles.
Guangzhou Auto hopes to become one of a handful of auto-making conglomerates that emerge in China in the coming decade. 
Officials in Beijing have said they hope to consolidate the nation's 123 auto assembly plants into a dozen companies as part of an overall plan to make the nation's cumbersome state-run industry more efficient.
Though its potential is tantalizingly large, China's auto market is still relatively small. 
Passenger cars account for only about a quarter of the 1.5 million vehicles assembled here, which are mostly trucks and vans.
One perennially touchy issue in China's car manufacturing is the amount of local content in autos made by international car makers. 
Honda said 40 percent of the China-made Accords would be made with local components in the first year, though that number is expected to rise in subsequent years.
Required to work with a local partner, international auto makers have rarely been able to profit in China. 
The outlook for car makers has grown hazier in recent months, as car sales have dropped, and the recent economic downturn in Southeast Asia is not expected to help.
By contrast, Honda's most lucrative markets are in the West, which was reflected in the six-month earnings report the company released today. 
Helped by the diminished value of the yen, Honda's exports almost doubled to meet strong demand in Europe and the United States. 
Honda vehicle sales rose 16 percent in the United States, to about half a million. 
A popular seller was the CR-V sport utility vehicle, which Honda began selling in the United States in February. 
European buyers snapped up CR-V's and Civics.
The export markets compensated for weak sales in Japan. 
Like Japan's other car manufacturers, Honda has been hurt by an increase in the Japanese sales tax, the elimination of tax rebates and an increase in health insurance premiums. 
Also, mini-cars, which produce less profit, are accounting for a bigger portion of Honda's domestic sales.
In the fiscal first half, which ended Sept. 
30, net income rose to 126.49 billion yen, or $1.02 billion, from 94.91 billion yen a year earlier. 
Sales increased 13 percent, to 2.794 trillion yen from 2.479 trillion yen.
Honda also acknowledged that the Southeast Asian economic crisis would hurt its sales in the region. 
It lowered its full-year forecast for production in Asia outside of Japan by 30 percent, to 130,000 units. 
But it raised its full-year export target by 21 percent, to 570,000 autos.

file: INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS_China and South Korea End Talks on Jet.txt
text:
ï»¿
Talks between South Korea and China on a project to develop passenger jets collapsed today.
An official at the South Korean Trade Ministry said the negotiations in Beijing, which opened on Monday, had broken down over differences on where to base final production.
China demanded that the assembly line be in Shanghai, while South Korea pressed for split production between the two countries, he said. 
Beijing officials also tried to reduce South Korea's stake in the project.
The breakdown in the talks could signal the start of a competition between China and South Korea to become the first to build a midsized passenger jet. 
The two countries agreed in March 1994 to jointly develop a 100-seat passenger jet.
Samsung Aerospace, a unit of the giant Samsung industrial group, was to be the lead company in the South Korean consortium, which also included Daewoo Heavy Industries, the Korean Airlines Company, the Hyundai Aerospace Industrial Company and the Goldstar Precision Company.

file: INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS_Dana to Build Plant in China.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Dana Corporation, a maker of auto parts, said yesterday that it would build an axle factory in China's Fujian province, part of the company's efforts to offer customers in the Asia-Pacific region better support.
Dana, which is based in Toledo, Ohio, already operates three manufacturing plants in China and 13 in the Asia-Pacific region.
Dana's Fujian Spicer Drivetrain Systems unit will build the 40,000-square-foot plant in Fuzhou. 
The plant, scheduled for completion next summer, will eventually employ about 150 workers. 
The company did not disclose the amount of its investment.
Initially, the plant is to make axle parts for full-size and small vans and sell them to a Fujian-based vehicle assembler. 
Later, it will make front and rear axles for light-duty vehicles.

ï»¿
Kawasaki of Japan is prepared to license a Macao-Chinese joint venture called the Benteng Motorcycle Company to produce 300,000 of its motorcycles annually in South China by 1996, the official newspaper China Daily reported today.
Benteng will build a $138 million factory in the Zhuhai Special Economic Zone, in the booming southern province of Guangdong, to produce 100cc, 125cc and 250cc Kawasaki motorcycles, a Benteng official told the paper.
Honda, Yamaha, Suzuki of Japan, Kwang Yang Motor Company, Sanyang of Taiwan and the Chia Tai Group of Thailand have all already set up joint motorcycle ventures in China.
Despite China's huge population, there are only eight million motorcycles on Chinese roads and annual production is fewer than two million a year. 
Motorbikes are starting to cram roads in booming south China, however, where licensing restrictions on private motorbike ownership have gradually been eased.
Kawasaki signed a technical cooperation agreement with Benteng in July and a contract will be signed soon, Lu Zhongyin, the Benteng vice president, told the paper. 
The paper did not say who are Benteng's shareholders.
Kawasaki will initially supply most of the parts for the bikes, but after 1996 Benteng expects to be able to produce engines, the paper said.

file: Nissan Is Approved For China Venture.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Nissan Motor Company announced today that it had received the Chinese Government's approval for the manufacturing and marketing of commercial vehicles in a joint venture in China's Zhengzhou City.
The joint venture, the Zhengzhou Nissan Automobile Company, in which the No. 2 Japanese auto maker has a 5 percent share, will manufacture 5,000 Nissan pickup trucks this year. 
The output is expected to rise to 50,000 by 2000.
For Nissan, the Zhengzhou joint venture is the first vehicle manufacturing project in which it has its own share. 
"This is our first step into China's commercial vehicle production," a spokesman said.
The Nissan Diesel Motor Company announced a truck and bus project in China's Zhejiang province last month, but it involves bigger vehicles.
Nissan had first announced the plan for the Zhengzhou joint venture in March 1993 and the partners started building 200 to 300 vehicles monthly on a test basis late last year, the Nissan spokesman said.

file: The Race Begins to Build a Small Car for China.txt
text:
ï»¿
General Motors said today that it would begin producing a small car in China in December, the first of several such offerings planned by some of the world's largest automakers, each hoping to dominate this country's potentially huge market.
Based on the Opel Corsa that G.M. makes in Brazil, the car will be sold under the Buick brand and will be called the Sail in English, a transliteration of its Chinese name, Sai Ou, which means roughly "compete with Europe."
General Motors' China operations expect to face competition from European as well as American and Japanese manufacturers after China joins the World Trade Organization and car import duties fall.
The first Sail is scheduled to roll off the production line on Dec. 
12 at the company's Shanghai joint venture with the state-owned Shanghai Automotive Industrial Corporation. 
Full production is to begin next April.
Many automakers have exhibited prototypes of family cars for the China market, and several have announced their intention to offer models in the $12,000 price range -- the market segment at which the government wants to aim. 
Volkswagen is expected to introduce a version of the Polo at its joint venture with Shanghai Automotive. 
Toyota is expected to announce a version of its Yaris at a joint venture in Tianjin, a huge industrial city in the northeast. 
And Ford is in negotiations with a Chinese carmaker in Sichuan province to produce a small, inexpensive car.
Despite its obvious promise, China's car market has been slow to develop because the government has preferred that tax revenue and people's savings flow elsewhere -- into the country's fledgling private housing market, for example.
China's network of roads had been considered too undeveloped to support the explosion of traffic that private car ownership will bring. 
And the government has been reluctant to allow foreigners to dominate such a major industry as automaking.
But all this is changing, in large part because of the pressures that global trade membership will bring. 
China will have to open its market to car imports after it joins the W.T.O. 
-- a move expected within the next few months -- and it is relaxing restrictions on the industry now to give domestic manufacturers a chance to prepare. 
In the country's coming five-year plan, the blueprint that will guide government economic policy from 2001 through 2005, the automobile industry's ranking is expected to edge ahead of that of housing.
Thanks to heavy government spending to keep the economy chugging in recent years, a national network of highways now links most of the country's cities.
And while many cities can ill afford more cars on their already jammed roads, officials hope that car sales will help stimulate consumer spending and "turn auto consumption into a major driver of China's economic growth," said the president of Shanghai General Motors, Chen Hong.
Demand is greatest for inexpensive cars of high quality.
"If your intent is to be No. 1 in China, you'd better be No. 1 in this segment," said Michael J. Dunne, president of Automotive Resources Asia, a marketing services company with offices in Beijing. 
He estimates that by 2005, half of all cars sold in China will be in this market segment, sold to members of the urban middle class.
Private car ownership was almost unheard of a decade ago; five years ago, it accounted for only 10 percent of new car sales. 
But that share has risen since the Asian economic crisis rattled regional economies, and China, trying to increase consumer spending to keep its economy stable, began encouraging people to use their cash. 
Private buyers now account for 40 percent of new car sales, and Mr. Dunne estimates that that will rise to 60 percent or higher by 2005, even as competition will keep prices low and profit margins thin. 
"Market share is the name of the game," he said.
This is not the fabled billion-buyer market; much of the purchasing has been in the countryside, where small-time entrepreneurs buy tiny, tinny vehicles that sell for $3,000 to $5,000 each.
In the cities, though, there are plenty of high-salary office workers and young entrepreneurs who would like to own a higher-quality car but cannot afford the sedans now available.
"I've encouraged my staff to buy cars, but right now there are really no affordable cars to choose from," said Wei Wei, who owns a garment-exporting business in Shanghai and who herself has yet to buy a car, though she has had a driver's license for years.
Ms. Wei said she was planning to buy a Buick sedan, currently G.M.'s main product at its Shanghai plant. 
Such cars generally start around $35,000.
The Sail, however, is the company's best chance at making full use of its sprawling $1.52 billion joint-venture factory in Shanghai. 
While the venture announced a profit of $72 million last year, sales have failed to meet expectations. 
The plant, with the capacity to make 100,000 cars a year, began producing a minivan in April that has not sold well. 
And the factory will turn out only 30,000 to 35,000 vehicles this year, far short of the 50,000 the company forecast.
"We're pretty excited about the opportunity in the small-car market," said Philip Murtaugh, chairman and chief executive of G.M. 
China.
The country's anticipated entry into the World Trade Organization has hurt Shanghai G.M.'s sales because many Chinese have put off car purchases, expecting prices to fall after the drop in import duties pushes prices down. 
The slump in sales set off an industry price war that hurt G.M. further.
Competition has also chewed away at some of the Buick's market, which appeared wide open when the joint venture was originally formed in the mid-90's. 
Honda has begun offering an Accord model built at a plant in Guangzhou, in the south. 
And Shanghai Automotive's joint venture with Volkswagen, also in Shanghai, began offering a slightly smaller Passat model this year. 
Shanghai VW is expected to begin producing a 3-liter Passat intended to compete directly with Shanghai G.M.'s Buick sometime in 2001.
At a trade fair here on Tuesday, Shanghai G.M. will display two of its new Opel-derivative Sail cars assembled from kits imported from Brazil. 
The 1.6-liter Sail will come with safety features currently unheard of in China's bare-bones small-car market. 
Those include driver- and passenger-side air bags, four-wheel antilock brakes, a safety cage built into the body, and shock-absorbing front and rear crush zones.

The Toshiba Corporation said today that it would set up a 60-percent-owned joint venture in China to produce semiconductors for televisions and audio equipment. 
Under an agreement with the Huajin Electronics Group Corporation, China's leading maker of integrated circuits, the $10 million plant will be set up in Wuxi in Jiansu Province, north of Shanghai, in October.
